What this project does

Nestlé Brazil is deploying image recognition to automate the capture of in-store merchandising indicators. Merchandisers photograph the shelf. The system reads the photo and returns share of shelf, facings, out of stock and distribution by SKU, replacing manual survey entry.

Business Objectives

  • Increase visibility of point of sale execution.
  • Automate capture of merchandising indicators.
  • Improve data quality and reliability.
  • Cut the time employees spend on manual surveys.
  • Enable faster data driven decisions.
  • Find opportunities to grow share of space and exposure.
  • Support category growth through better execution.

Expected Outcomes

  • Feed existing Power BI reports.
  • Monitor KPIs continuously.
  • Identify opportunities by store, region and category.
  • Data driven action plans for field teams.
  • Validate planogram implementation.
  • Track campaigns and point of sale materials.

Value by Role

Merchandiser Less time on surveys. Less manual data entry. More focus on execution and selling.
Field Leader Real time visibility of indicators. Better visit prioritisation and coaching.

Known problems this addresses

Execution Issues

  • Out of stock on leading SKUs, especially at peak hours.
  • Mismatch between planogram and actual execution.
  • Low visibility on shelves and secondary displays.
  • No replenishment during high traffic periods.

Measurement Issues

  • Difficulty auditing execution at scale.
  • Inconsistency in manual data collection.
  • Execution varies significantly store to store, which distorts visibility and share of space reads.

Channel Context

A&A, Wholesale High turnover categories such as Chocolates and Biscuits become disorganised through the day. Smaller packs lose alignment fastest. Out of stock on leading SKUs is common at peak hours.
AS / Impulse, Convenience & Immediate Consumption Coffee is usually better organised. Chocolates and checkout items need frequent replenishment. Execution quality varies widely across stores.

A day in the life of a merchandiser

Current process, from the Market Discovery submission.

  • Arrives at the store and checks in.
  • Identifies the categories under their responsibility: Chocolates, Biscuits, Coffee, Powdered Beverages and others.
  • Assesses product availability on shelves, secondary displays and checkout areas.
  • Replenishes and organises products against the planogram.
  • Corrects out of stock situations and checks replenishment opportunities.
  • Captures photos of categories and execution points using the app.
  • Answers operational surveys and records incidents.
  • Completes the visit and checks out.
Where TIR changes this Photo capture stays. The survey answering step shrinks. Collection time for manual versus automated capture will be measured through the pilot to quantify the efficiency gain and error reduction.

Pilot Configuration

The 127 SKU set is the pilot itself, not a subset of it. Nestlé expects to launch with all 127 from day one.

Competitor Recognition

Approach

  • Capture competitor products to calculate share of shelf.
  • Measure presence, exposure and occupied space.
  • Recognise competitors at SKU level, not brand level.
  • Enable comparative execution analysis.

Why it matters

  • Share of shelf is meaningless without the denominator. Competitor facings are that denominator.
  • Supports commercial decisions and merchandising strategy against competitive dynamics.

Scale beyond the pilot

Rollout scope is materially larger than the pilot and not yet planned in detail.

  • Full Brazil expansion is estimated at more than 3,000 SKUs including competitor products.
  • The 2 week training cycle is the current planning assumption per category. Whether it holds at rollout volume is an open question with the image recognition provider.
  • Rollout is expected to be phased in batches or waves rather than a single release.
  • Nestlé Brazil introduces innovation SKUs every quarter. The incremental training time for a small new SKU batch is not yet known.
Steering decision at kick-off Paulo Miranda directed the team to keep expansion questions separate from pilot execution so the pilot keeps its discipline. Scaling questions will be answered by TELUS at the appropriate time.

KPIs

KPIBasisOperational Definition
Share of Shelf% of facingsMeasures the percentage of shelf space your products occupy relative to total available space. Calculated at category or brand level using facings as the basis.
Out of StockPer SKUFlags products missing from shelf that are part of the customer assortment. Only assortment-listed products are evaluated for out-of-stock status.
FacingsCountCounts visible product units in the front row of a shelf. Only front-row products are counted, regardless of units stacked behind.
Calculation basis confirmed Share of shelf is measured by percentage of facings. Linear space measurement is out of scope.

Reporting

Reports in use today

  • Power BI dashboards for field execution.
  • Out of stock dashboard.
  • Share of facings dashboard.
  • Coverage and effectiveness reports.
  • Time spent on surveys.

Business Rules Definition Session

Working session held 10 September 2026. SSBS presented the image recognition edge cases and limitations. Nestlé Brazil confirmed how each case should be treated. TELUS chaired and translated. The session ran mostly in Portuguese; all rules below are recorded in English.

TELUS Jaziel Damian (chair), David Kimm, Marcela Gonzalez, JC Attipalli
Nestlé Brazil Patricia Ferraresso, Higor Gomes, Lucas Marinelli
SSBS Mariana Halyk, Anna Babukhina, Roman Naida
Purpose Lock the counting and recognition rules before the IR Business Blueprint is written, so the tool behaves the same way in production as it does in the pilot. These rules are the business rules scope freeze.

The core counting rule

Two decisions govern every other rule on this page. Both were confirmed in session by Patricia Ferraresso and David Kimm.

One visible unit equals one facing Each product unit with a visible unique identifier is counted as its own facing. A vertical column of units is not collapsed into a single facing. Confirmed on the reconfirmation raised by Anna Babukhina at the close of the session.
Front row only Only the first level of product is counted. Units stacked or stored behind the front row are excluded, regardless of how many are there. Nestlé asked for this to be standard across all four categories.
Recognition floor The tool recognises a unit when more than 50 percent of the front face is visible and the unique identifier can be read. Below that, the unit is not counted. Where only part of the identifier is visible, SSBS can often read brand and flavour but not grammage, so SKU level recognition is not guaranteed.

Cross-category recognition rules

Rules that apply to Chocolates, Coffee, Powdered Beverages and Biscuits alike.

CaseTool behaviourNestlé decision
Stacked productsEach unit is recognised separately when more than 50 percent of the front face and the unique identifier are visible.Count one facing per visible unit, not one per column. Confirmed
Partially covered productsOnly units with a visible face are recognised. Units fully covered by another item are not returned.Rule accepted as stated. No change requested. Confirmed
No visible unique identifierBrand and sometimes flavour can be read. Grammage often cannot, so the SKU cannot be resolved.SSBS cannot commit to recognising these units. Accepted as a known limitation. Confirmed
Products in bulkRecognition degrades when products are loose and unaligned.Field team to arrange products before the photo. Confirmed
Side-facing productsSide panels usually lack the identifiers needed for SKU level recognition.Field team to turn products front-facing before the photo. Confirmed
Fallen or knocked over productsNot reliably recognised in that position.Field team to reposition before the photo. Confirmed
Products at the back of the shelfRecognition accuracy drops with depth and obstruction.Field team to pull product forward before the photo. Excluded from the facing count either way, under the front row rule. Confirmed
Products upside downIdentifier orientation reduces recognition precision. No guarantee.Field team to correct orientation before the photo. Confirmed
Products at an angle, roughly 45 degreesAngled placement is not guaranteed to be recognised.Recommendation accepted. Field team to square products to the shelf. Confirmed
Closed boxesContents cannot be identified.Excluded. Nestlé counts products on the shelf only, never closed boxes. Confirmed
Empty boxesNo product to recognise.Excluded from recognition and from share of shelf. Nestlé does not use empty boxes in the calculation. Confirmed
Same design, multiple weightsPacks that share artwork across grammages are hard to separate visually.Group them into one category. Applied consistently wherever this pattern appears. Confirmed
Products turned backwardsRear panel does not carry the identifier.Field team to turn the pack to the front before the photo. Confirmed
Vertical and horizontal display of the same SKUBoth orientations are recognised when the identifiers are visible.Return one result per SKU. Vertical and horizontal facings are summed into a single figure, not split into two products. Confirmed

Category-specific decisions

Where a case was category specific, Nestlé chose the option that keeps behaviour consistent across all four categories.

CategoryCaseDecision
BiscuitsPacks laid sideways in vertical stacks, each with a visible unique identifierCount each pack as a separate facing.
BiscuitsWhich faces count when a pack shows more than one faceCount front-facing and side-facing units. Exclude the top face. Validate
BiscuitsIndividual packs with no distinguishing characteristicsNo recognition guarantee. Field team to ensure the identifier is visible.
BiscuitsEmpty boxes used as shelf fillersNot used for share of shelf. Excluded from recognition.
CoffeeJars turned so only the side panel is visibleField team to place jars facing front. Side panel alone is not sufficient.
CoffeeProducts covered, or arranged in a single rowRecommendation accepted as presented. No changes.
CoffeeProducts placed on top of the shelf unitNot recognised and not counted. Standardised with the other categories.
CoffeeWhether side-facing products are included in the countCount only products with the face turned to the front. Chosen for consistency across categories. Validate
ChocolatesIndividual sachets and single unitsLikely out of scope. These SKUs are not on the 127 SKU list Nestlé provided. To be reconfirmed against the final catalogue.
Two rules to validate against the SSBS deck The Biscuits decision counts side faces. The Coffee decision counts front faces only. Both are marked above. Confirm the intended behaviour with SSBS before the business rules freeze, so the blueprint does not carry a contradiction.

Promotional and seasonal packaging

Nestlé position

  • Promotional and seasonal variants are treated as separate products, not as variants of the base SKU.
  • Brazil runs campaign packaging through the year, so this is a recurring case, not an exception.

SSBS position

  • A promotional design is recognised only if it is in the catalogue and the model has been trained on it.
  • Any design change that alters the unique identifier requires the new design to be trained.
  • Minor design changes may still be recognised, but accuracy is not guaranteed.
Nestlé dependency For every promotional or seasonal SKU, Nestlé must supply the artwork and the SKU name as it appears in the product catalogue. SSBS cannot start training without both. This becomes a standing operational commitment once the pilot goes live, not a one-time handover.

Scope clarifications from the checklist

TopicOutcome
Impulse channelIn scope. Convenience formats such as petrol station and transit station stores, carrying impulse purchase items including chocolate bars and ready to drink products. Share of shelf is calculated for this channel as well, not recognition only.
Secondary displaysOut of scope. No longer applicable to the pilot. Gondola only, as recorded in Scope & Pilot.
Pilot usersApproximately 125 users, derived from the monthly route plan. Confirmed to SSBS in session.
Share of shelf calculationSSBS applies a grid approach where one unit equals one facing. TELUS will issue the standard KPI calculation documentation, Nestlé approves it, then TELUS confirms it to SSBS as the standard to build against.
MSL productsSSBS could not locate the MSL products in the catalogue provided. Still open. The MSL drives distribution and out of stock, so it blocks those KPIs.
Rollout scope questionsDeferred. Jaziel moved rollout discussion out of this session to keep the focus on the pilot. To be handled with the leadership team.
Out of stock and remaining process itemsDeferred to an offline TELUS and SSBS working session. Anna asked which business processes image recognition results feed into. TELUS to answer from the Discovery output and come back to SSBS.

ActionOwnerNote

Where the risk actually sits Most of these rules are recommendations to the field, not tool settings. The tool will report what the photo shows. If merchandisers do not front-face, square and clear the shelf before capture, the accuracy numbers in the pilot will measure execution discipline rather than recognition quality. Brief the field team before the first category goes live, with the lead time Caroline Venancio asked for at kick-off.

Category Release Sequence

Categories are trained and released one at a time. Each finished category goes to the field for testing while the next is still training.

StepDetail
Training cycleTwo weeks of neural training per category, confirmed by TELUS at kick-off.
Expected paceRoughly one new category available to the field every two weeks, assuming no rework.
Rework riskPhotos may be rejected and need recapture, which extends the cycle. Two weeks is the ideal case, not a guarantee.
Go-live datesPer-category go-live dates will be in the project plan, so the field team knows the schedule in advance.
Field noticeThe field team must be told as early as possible before any test window. They run multiple concurrent research programmes and cannot absorb short-notice requests.
Constraint raised by Caroline Venancio Do not ask the field team on a Friday to start testing on Monday. Any activity that involves the business and field testing needs maximum advance notice. This is a scheduling dependency, not a preference.

On-shelf photo quality

SSBS has reviewed the on-shelf photos supplied for Brazil and found quality problems: blurred images, glare, and shots taken at an angle rather than square to the shelf at the required distance. SSBS is preparing a findings pack with examples.

If a new or supplementary photo set is required, the field capture sits outside this plan and adds time before the 24 September catalogue approval can be given. The volume affected will be known when the findings pack is shared.

Next step: review the findings pack with Nestlé Brazil, agree the photo standard, and confirm whether a re-capture is needed. Decide this before the workshops so the schedule reflects it.

What this project does

Nestlé Ecuador is deploying Image Recognition to digitize and automate the capture of in-store execution indicators. Promoters photograph the gondola shelf, and the image recognition engine returns granular SKU-level share of shelf, facings count, and out-of-stock visibility into the existing TELUS / Power BI ecosystem.

Business Objectives

  • Digitize point-of-sale data collection with automated image auditing.
  • Transition measurement from total brand level to flavor/variant SKU level (e.g., Amor Chocolate vs. Amor Lemon).
  • Eliminate manual facing counting fatigue and human survey bias.
  • Protect and expand category leadership across key subcategories.
  • Standardize merchandising execution data across modern and traditional trade.
  • Maintain existing mature retail KPIs while drastically reducing promoter capture time.

Expected Outcomes

  • Direct automated feed into existing internal dashboards (Power BI / TELUS).
  • Benchmarked recognition accuracy target of 95% across primary packaging.
  • Granular Share of Shelf (SOS) visibility across leading flavors and packs.
  • Seamless operational synergy with internal alert systems such as SRE.
  • Rigorous execution compliance validation across major retail partners.

Value by Role

Merchandisers Adopt and properly execute the RIR solution in daily store routines. Improve shelf-image capture consistency while eliminating manual facing counts and survey fatigue.
Supervisors Monitor tool adoption and field execution quality. Perform image-based audits and validations across assigned doors, accelerating compliance visibility.
Coordinators Govern operational field processes and scheduled routines. Monitor project performance and compliance indicators to ensure consistent execution standards.
Business & Commercial Leadership Digitize shelf execution measurement, automate Share of Shelf calculations, unlock flavor/SKU-level performance, and establish the baseline for future category expansion.

Market Context & Key Nuances

Market Leadership Context

  • 50% Modern Trade Share: Modern trade accounts for 50% of total Nestlé Ecuador sales, with 85% total field coverage.
  • Leader in 70% of Categories: Nestlé holds clear market leadership (e.g., Amor brand drives 60–65% share of shelf in Wafers).
  • Mature Operating Model: Field routines and FEX auditing standards are highly sophisticated; TIR does not introduce new KPIs, but elevates capture speed and fidelity.

Operational Risks & Retail Constraints

  • Store Photography Permissions: Major chains such as Corporación Favorita (Supermaxi, representing ~60% of modern trade) have strict formal restrictions against camera capture. Promoters capture discretely or formal leadership negotiations will be required before rollout.
  • Narrow Aisle Geometry: Certain store formats have narrow aisle clearance (<1.0m–1.5m), requiring multi-shot stitched capture.
  • Cart and Shopper Obstructions: High-traffic periods cause physical blockages in front of extensive wafer displays.

A day in the life of a merchandiser (Embajador)

Field workflow documented during the Discovery Workshop by Diana Alvarez and Juan Carlos Espinosa.

  • Arrives at the store and inspects backroom storage (bodega) for incoming cases and transit orders.
  • Replenishes primary linear gondolas (lineales) first, followed by promotional endcaps (cabeceras).
  • Conducts price tag and promo sweep, ensuring promotional signage and discount tags match current campaigns.
  • Opens the mobile app to review stock-outs (quiebres de stock), blocked SKUs, and pending warehouse orders.
  • Executes the Share of Shelf (SOS) routine (currently manual, transitioning to automated photo capture).
  • Assembles secondary promotional islands, rumbas, or pallet displays per monthly trade marketing focus.
  • Completes in-store administrative checklist and clocks out to next route destination.
How TIR Transforms the Routine Manual facing counts per competitor SKU are eliminated. The embajador captures overlapping panorama photos of the wafer and culinary gondola. The IR engine parses facings automatically, saving approximately 15–20 minutes per complex category audit.

Pilot Configuration

The Ecuador pilot is strictly calibrated to 2 high-volume subcategories across 70 Modern Trade outlets in Corporación El Rosado.

ParameterEcuador Pilot Specification
Retail ChainCorporación El Rosado (Mi Comisariato / Hipermarket) - 70 designated pilot stores.
ChannelsModern Trade (Supermarkets) for Pilot. Traditional Trade (tiendas de barrio) planned for Rollout.
In-Store ScopePrimary shelf only. Secondary displays, floor pallets, and coolers are strictly out of scope.
Pilot Subcategories1. Wafers and 2. Mayonnaise.
Pilot Core SKUs~40 Wafer SKUs and ~60 Mayonnaise SKUs, representing 95% of category sales volume
Active Mobile Users34 Field Users (combination of Merchandizers, Supervisors, and Field Coordinators).
Corporate DevicesSamsung Galaxy A20 & Galaxy A22 enterprise fleet running Android OS.
Visit Frequency1 official SOS visit per month standard; 2 to 3 visits per month during pilot to maximize sample volume.
Photos per VisitAverage of 6 photos per visit (~3 per subcategory anaquel; max 8 on very wide gondolas).

Packaging Types in Pilot

FLEXIBLE FILMS (FLOW PACKS)

  • Category: Wafer
  • Challenges: Glossy reflective film surfaces; packs laid flat or sideways; orientation shifts during high-traffic hours.
  • Guideline: Standardize model training on both front face and primary side panel artwork.

DOYPACKS (STAND-UP POUCHES)

  • Category: Mayonnaise
  • Features: Flexible pouch packaging with prominent upper spout and center branding.
  • Guideline: Front vertical posture is standard; pouch deformations must be accounted for in training imagery.

Competitor Recognition Strategy

Approach

  • Recognition at SKU level, not merely aggregate brand level.
  • Filter scope to the top competitor SKUs accounting for 95% category volume.
  • Includes direct wafer challengers and national/multinational mayonnaise brands.
  • Competitor packshot artwork curated from web catalogs and in-store high-res captures.

Commercial Impact

  • Accurate denominator: Share of Shelf requires absolute facing counts of competitive products.
  • Validates promotional expansions and competitive encroachments on eye-level shelves.
  • Eliminates human estimation bias when counting competitive multi-pack variants.

Shelf Placement & Facing Counting Rules

Specific execution decisions governing how packaged goods are recognized across retail fixtures.

ConditionTool Recognition BehaviorNestlé Ecuador Decision
Wafers Stacked Horizontally Individual horizontal flow packs stacked in layers without tray dividers. Count as 1 Facing per column / arrangement. A stack of 4–6 horizontal wafer packs represents a single facing.
Wafers 1 Over 2 Flat 1 upright front-facing wafer placed over 2 horizontal base packs. Count as 1 Facing. Treated as a single facing group in accordance with retail execution standards.
Mayonnaise Doypacks Flexible stand-up pouches with spout caps placed in front row. One unit equals one facing. Standard 1:1 facing count for fronted pouches.
Price Tags (Flejes / Etiquetas) Visible price labels and promotional tags along the shelf rail. Captured but excluded from KPIs. Price tags will be visible in photos but are not measured as active objects.
Gondola Only Scope Secondary pallet displays, checkout chillers, and side hanging strips. Excluded from pilot. Photos are taken exclusively on primary ambient gondolas (lineales/perchas).
Wide Gondola Panoramic Stitched Shots Large wafer displays spanning multiple modular bodies (cuerpos). Puzzle / Stitched Capture. Promoters take 2–3 overlapping continuous shots (~6 total) stitched seamlessly by the mobile app.
Partially Obscured Packs Unit blocked by shopper cart, promoter hands, or pillar. Recognition requires >50% of the brand artwork face to resolve SKU identity. Field team trained to clear obstructions.

Rollout Scale Horizon

The production rollout across Ecuador represents an order of magnitude expansion following pilot stabilization.

Rollout DimensionProjected Production Scale
Store Universe700 stores across Modern Trade and key Traditional Trade routes.
Active User Fleet~160 total users (140 Merchandisers, 13 Supervisors, 4 Coordinators, plus Field Management).
Subcategories21 to 22 subcategories (encompassing full Culinary, Biscuits, Dairy, Coffee, and Nature's Heart).
Total SKU Universe~1,100 to 1,200 SKUs (~300 Nestlé SKUs + ~800 to 900 Competitor SKUs).
Monthly Photos~60 photos per visit average (~70–80 max in hypermarkets) across scheduled route visits.
Executive Guidance Rollout planning and commercial expansions will remain decoupled from pilot execution until pilot KPIs and 95% accuracy thresholds are proven in the 70 El Rosado stores.

KPIs

KPI Basis Operational Definition
Share of Shelf % of facings Measures the percentage of shelf space your products occupy relative to total available space. Calculated at category or brand level using facings as the basis.
Out of Stock Per SKU Flags products missing from shelf that are part of the customer assortment. Only assortment-listed products are evaluated for out-of-stock status.
Facings Count Counts visible product units in the front row of a shelf. Only front-row products are counted, regardless of units stacked behind.
CALCULATION BASIS CONFIRMED Share of shelf is strictly measured by percentage of product facings. Linear space measurement is out of scope for Ecuador.

Reporting & System Integration

Dashboards Fed Today

  • Power BI Field Execution Dashboard.
  • Weekly Out of Stock (OSA) monitoring report.
  • Subcategory Share of Shelf comparative reports.
  • Store visit compliance & coverage dashboards.

System Synergy

  • TELUS Platform: Seamless automated data ingestion to replace manual survey inputs.
  • SRE Integration: Complements existing POS alert tools (phantom inventory, phantom stock-outs, demand surges).
  • SKU Breakdown: Unlocks sub-brand SKU reporting (e.g., Amor Chocolate vs. Amor Vanilla market share).

Prerequisites for Feasibility Study

The 3 mandatory gating items required before TELUS and SSBS initiate the 2-week Feasibility Study.

DeliverableTarget DateStatus & Detail
1. Core SKU Catalog 17 Sep 2026 Final list of ~40 Wafer and ~60 Mayonnaise SKUs (Nestlé + competitor 95% volume) filtered and agreed.
2. Packshot Artwork 17 Sep 2026 100% Nestlé packshots delivered; remaining competitor packaging photos/packshots collated.
3. On-Shelf Sample Photos Week of 21 Sep 2026 High-quality real store gondola captures across El Rosado outlets for AI baseline validation.
Photo Quality Mandate Learning from prior Latin American rollouts: blurry, reflective, or obstructed initial photos cause cycle rework. Field promoters must ensure crisp illumination and minimum 1.0m distance.

Risks & Mitigation Plan

Identified operational, technical, and commercial risks with agreed mitigation actions.

RiskImpactMitigation Strategy
Poor quality shelf photos Rework, model degradation, and delays in feasibility analysis. Perform structured quality validation before submission to ensure clarity, proper lighting, and minimum 1.0m distance.
Incomplete SKU catalog Delays in model training and recognition engine setup. Execute thorough local business validation across Wafer and Mayonnaise prior to package handover.
Complex shelf presentations Recognition challenges and reduced facing accuracy in Wafers. Explicitly address multi-pack and stacked arrangements during the 2-week technical feasibility assessment.
Retail photography permissions Operational restrictions in key chains (e.g., Favorita ~60% MT). Engage retail account leadership formally to secure protocol alignment prior to broader deployment.
User adoption & consistency Reduced solution effectiveness and uneven data quality. Establish structured promoter training, supervisory audit routines, and regular governance reviews.
Store layout variability Inconsistent photo capture quality across narrow aisles. Publish standardized image capture guidelines and utilize the application's panoramic stitched capture mode.

  • Final SKU catalog: ~40 Wafer and ~60 Mayonnaise SKUs locked.
  • Packshots completed: 100% Nestlé and competitive packaging gathered.

What this project does

Nestlé Panama is deploying TELUS Image Recognition (TIR) to automate point-of-sale shelf auditing in Modern Trade. Merchandisers capture stationary overlapping photographs of primary ambient gondolas, and the computer vision engine calculates SKU-level facing counts, Share of Shelf (SOS), and empty facings, streaming structured raw data directly into Panama's Snowflake data warehouse.

Business Objectives

  • Automate manual shelf auditing: Eliminate tedious manual facing counts and manual survey questionnaires during daily store visits.
  • Liberate supervisory bandwidth: Free field supervisors from manual linear measurements to focus on high-value merchandising coaching and store execution quality.
  • Establish daily facing-level share visibility: Gain granular, daily SKU-level Share of Shelf (SOS) against competitors across leading supermarket chains.
  • Protect category leadership: Monitor assortment compliance, promotional execution, and out-of-stock gaps in real time across flagship culinary categories.
  • Unify multi-country cluster assets: Lay the foundation for Central American homologation across Panama, Costa Rica, Honduras, and Nicaragua.

Expected Outcomes

  • Direct automated feed into Panama's existing Snowflake and Power BI analytical reports.
  • Benchmarked recognition accuracy target exceeding 95% on primary shelf packaging.
  • Daily visibility into empty facings (OOS) and competitor encroachment without manual audit bias.
  • Significantly reduced promoter in-store dwell time on surveys, redirecting effort toward shelf restocking and FEFO rotation.
  • Optimized cost structure through regional SKU artwork reuse across identical Central American packaging.

Value by Role

Merchandisers Adopt intuitive mobile image capture. Eliminate manual counting fatigue, reduce survey completion time, and regain focus on core restocking, product rotation (FEFO), and display cleanliness.
Supervisors Relieved from manual facing surveys. Shift supervisory focus to high-impact operational auditing, field coaching, and ensuring execution standards across their assigned promoter door rosters.
Coordinators & Operations Monitor project adoption and photo capture quality in real time. Maintain disciplined data collection standards and govern operational workflows via existing TELUS RE tools.
Commercial & Business Leadership Gain daily visibility into shelf execution metrics, unlock granular competitor facing comparisons, and leverage regional cluster synergies to scale TIR across Central America cost-effectively.

Market Context & Key Constraints

Fragmented Retail Landscape

  • No Dominant Monolithic Chain: Unlike other Central American or South American markets, Panama has no Walmart. Retail is fragmented across ~6 major competitive chains (including Super 99, El Machetazo, Riba Smith, and Rey).
  • Retailer-Controlled Planograms: Only ~2 supermarket chains allow Nestlé to enforce its own "Picture of Success". In remaining chains, the retailer or category leader dictates the planogram, causing significant display variations even within identical store footprints.
  • Dynamic Chain Pricing: Independent chains adjust consumer prices frequently to compete against one another, requiring diligent field monitoring.

Operational & Safety Constraints

  • Safety Directives: Strict Nestlé occupational health guidelines prohibit merchandisers from walking while filming or holding mobile devices. Promoters must stand stationary, face the shelf squarely, and shoot stationary modular frames.
  • Restricted Photography Stores: A small subset of store locations enforce strict device restrictions. These doors are proactively excluded from the pilot scope upfront.
  • Enterprise Connectivity: 100% of pilot mobile users operate new Samsung Galaxy A36 handsets backed by unlimited cellular data packages, ensuring reliable daily uploads.

A day in the life of a merchandiser

Documented field workflow from the Discovery Workshop with Kevin Rodríguez and Jossue Aguilar.

  • Point of Sale Check-in: Arrives at store and registers arrival in TELUS RE with mandatory GPS geolocation and storefront photo verification.
  • Shelf Cleaning & Restocking: Cleans shelf space, verifies backroom storage, and replenishes missing products onto the primary gondola.
  • Current Photo Capture: Currently takes manual planimetry photos (primarily for static compliance records, with limited automated analytics).
  • Manual Stock-Out & Monitoring Sweep: Fills out manual monitoring forms in TELUS RE for out-of-stock items, price surveys, and expiry (FEFO) sweeps.
  • Promo & Secondary Display Sweep: Validates promotional offers via the TELUS RE recommendation module and takes photos of secondary displays (islands, endcaps, cross strips).
  • Incident Reporting & Check-out: Submits quality or SHE incident forms as needed, finishes the daily checklist, and clocks out to the next assignment.
How TIR Transforms the Routine TIR automates facing counts and shelf audits directly from 15–21 gondola photos. Manual questionnaire burden is eliminated, freeing up approximately 20–30 minutes per store for restocking, FIFO/FEFO date rotation, and promotional arrangement.

Pilot Configuration

The Panama pilot focuses on Modern Trade supermarkets across 150 outlets with dedicated 1:1 merchandiser coverage.

ParameterPanama Pilot Specification
Retail ChainsTop Modern Trade chains across Panama (~6 leading supermarket banners, including Super 99 and El Machetazo).
Sales ChannelsModern Trade (Supermarkets) only for pilot. Traditional Trade is strictly out of scope for Phase 1.
In-Store ScopePrimary shelf only. Secondary displays, floor pallets, coolers, endcaps, and cross strips are strictly out of scope.
Pilot Categories1. Maggi & 2. Leches Culinarias
Pilot Core SKUs~150 to 250 total SKUs from Maggi and Culinarios, TBC
Preliminary Market ScopePanama preliminary catalog spans ~6 categories and ~530 SKUs total (~600 SKUs max catalog), subject to final scope confirmation.
Active Mobile Users150 Field Users (1 merchandiser assigned per pilot store).
Corporate DevicesSamsung Galaxy A36 (8GB RAM version) enterprise fleet running modern Android OS with active unlimited cellular data.
Visit Frequency1 official visit per day per store (daily store maintenance routine).
Photos per VisitAverage of 15 photos per visit (~21 photos maximum for very wide main shelf layouts).

Packaging Types in Pilot

POUCHES, CARDBOARD & TRIPACKS

  • Category: Maggi
  • Challenges: Multi-unit shrink Tripacks (pasta + 2 sauce flavors, 100g); units placed in cardboard shelf shipper displays (cartoncitos).

METAL CANS & TETRA PACKS

  • Category: Leches Culinarias
  • Features: High uniformity; two primary industry can formats (large can and small can) across Nestlé and competitors.

Competitor Recognition Strategy

Approach

  • Recognition at SKU level (not aggregate brand level), ensuring granular flavor and packaging variant tracking.
  • Includes direct culinary competitors (tomato pastes, seasoned sauces, table sauces) and dairy competitors.
  • Competitor packshots sourced using high-res web scraping, AI Copilot assistance, and in-store field photo captures.

Commercial Impact

  • Establishes accurate facing denominators for Share of Shelf calculations across diverse competitor brands.
  • Detects competitor promotional encroachment on eye-level shelves across independent supermarket chains.
  • Provides audit-proof historical competitive benchmark data for trade marketing negotiations.

Shelf Placement & Facing Counting Rules

Execution decisions agreed during the Discovery Workshop for recognizing packaged goods on shelves.

ConditionTool Recognition BehaviorNestlé Panama Decision
Identical Stacked Units Multiple identical units stacked vertically on top of one another on a shelf tier. Count by unit / face. Every visible individual front-facing unit is counted as a facing.
Multipack Bundles (Tripacks) Shrink-wrapped promotional 3-pack bundles (e.g., Maggi paste + 2 flavored sauces, 100g). Count visible units. The tool identifies the distinct multipack SKU and tallies all visible front faces (3 visible units = 3 facings).
Cardboard Shipper Displays Factory display trays holding 6 sauce pouches placed directly onto gondola shelves. Recognized on shelf. The IR engine is trained to identify units even when the display lip occludes 10–15% of the lower face.
Closed Boxes Unopened master transit cartons resting in aisle or on lower tier. Excluded from recognition. Closed packaging is strictly out of scope.
Shelf Depth Units pushed back behind the primary front row. Front row only. TIR does not evaluate shelf depth; only front-row facings are audited.
Empty Facings Empty space on shelf rail assigned to an active assortment SKU. Empty Facing Flagged. Assortment gap detected and flagged as out-of-stock without manual survey prompts.
Price Tags Shelf edge price labels and promotional shelf talkers. Excluded from Phase 1. Captured in photo background but omitted from active measurement pending global homologation.
Capture Movement & Safety Merchandiser posture during image capture routine. Stationary Modular Capture. Walking video/panoramas strictly prohibited due to internal SHE regulations.

Regional Cluster Synergy & Rollout Horizon

Panama operates as part of the Central America & Caribbean (CARICAM) cluster with substantial opportunities for multi-country scale.

DimensionCARICAM Cluster Horizon
Total Market CatalogNestlé Panama catalog spans ~600 SKUs total across all categories.
Homologated SKUsMultiple categories share 100% identical packaging across CARICAM (e.g., 25 Nutrition SKUs originate from the same plant for all 6 countries).
Cluster Expansion (Central)Evaluating unified rollout across Cluster Central: Panama, Costa Rica, Honduras, and Nicaragua.
Volume Cost OptimizationVolume scaling lowers per-visit pricing significantly (from ~$1.30 down to ~$0.72 when exceeding 4,300 monthly visits).
Professional Services SharingSetup and training costs for shared SKUs and competitor models can be amortized across all 4 cluster markets.
Executive Alignment Panama serves as the lead market for the initial Proof of Value. Discussions are actively underway with regional leadership (Alessandra Escala, Rogerio, and Patricia Ferraresso) to determine whether CARICAM cluster countries will onboard jointly or in subsequent waves.

KPIs

KPI Basis Operational Definition
Empty Facing Empty slot count Flags unoccupied front-row positions assigned to customer-listed assortment items, automating out-of-stock detection without manual surveys.
Share of Shelf % of facings Measures the percentage of shelf facings occupied by Nestlé products relative to total category facings on primary gondolas. Calculated at category level.
CALCULATION BASIS CONFIRMED Share of shelf is strictly measured by percentage of product facings. Linear space measurement is out of scope for Panama Phase 1 due to lack of competitor dimension registries and additional processing cost.

Reporting & System Integration

In-House Data Pipeline

  • Snowflake Data Warehouse: TIR recognition results flow automatically from TELUS RE into Nestlé Panama's central Snowflake database.
  • Custom Power BI Dashboards: Panama's specialized business intelligence team handles all front-end dashboard visualization internally.
  • Dashboard Dependencies: No custom reporting needed from TELUS, only rapid reliable raw data ingestion.

Operational Synergies

  • Auditable Offer Validation: Image records confirm promotional activation for commercial audit compliance.
  • Price Survey Relief: Establishes future foundation to automate manual price monitoring once global homologation is finalized.
  • Supervisor Liberation: Supervisors transition from measuring facings manually to monitoring high-level compliance trends in Power BI.

DeliverableTarget TimelineStatus & Technical Detail
1. Core SKU Catalog End of September 2026 Finalized catalog of 150–250 SKUs across Maggi Culinarios and Leches Culinarias (Nestlé + competitors). Must include Product ID (PRD ID), Name, Category, and Brand. SAP ID alone is not acceptable.
2. Packshot Artwork End of September 2026 Minimum 1 frontal packshot image per SKU (multi-sided encouraged where available). Delivered directly as image files (no URL links) to SharePoint/Teams, with filenames strictly containing the TELUS RE PRD ID.
3. On-Shelf Sample Photos Early October 2026 At least 100 facing appearances per SKU in real gondola context (individual pack cutouts are prohibited). Photographed using 1 category per collection form without category mixing, following the 7 quality rules.
Gating Enforcement SSBS and TELUS will not schedule or initiate the 2-week technical Feasibility Study until all 3 deliverables are received and verified. This prevents model rework and timeline slippage observed in previous regional rollouts.

Risks & Mitigation Plan

Operational, technical, and commercial risks identified with agreed mitigation strategies.

RiskImpactMitigation Strategy
Inadequate SKU volume for pilot Under-representation of category behavior and sub-optimal AI model tuning. Combined Leches Culinarias with Maggi Culinarios to achieve the proven 150–250 SKU model training range.
Display shipper tray occlusion Cardboard lips occlude 10–15% of lower sauce pouch artwork. Include training imagery of pouches seated in original shipper trays so the model tolerates lower-edge occlusion.
Store planogram variability Disparate shelf placements across non-compliant supermarket chains. Train the model on pure visual packaging features rather than rigid spatial planograms; exclude camera-restricted stores upfront.
Occupational safety constraints Inability to capture fluid panoramic video sweeps while walking. Enforce stationary modular photo captures (15–21 shots) adhering strictly to Nestlé safety directives.
Pack redesign & SKU obsolescence Model recognition drops if packaging artwork changes post-training. Establish structured retraining protocol during maintenance support for redesigned consumer packaging.
Competitor packshot availability Difficulty obtaining pristine packaging artwork for third-party brands. Utilize automated web image harvesting, AI Copilot workflows, and high-resolution on-shelf captures.
